title: Identifiability of a linear dynamical reaction-diffusion system with directed interactions from the second-order statistics of a single snapshot
summary: A single spatial snapshot of a system with multiple interacting populations captures positions but not the underlying dynamics that have led to the observation. This work asks what the stationary second-order spatial statistics of a snapshot can reveal about the structure of the linear reaction-diffusion dynamical model, and in particular about the pairwise directed entries of its interaction operator. The observation is the matrix-valued structure factor $S(k)$ as a one-parameter family in the diffusion-inherited dependence on the wavenumber $κ=|k|^2$. The main result is that the directed interaction operator $A$ and the diffusivity matrix $D$ are generically identifiable for any number of interacting populations from $\{S(κ)\}$ up to a single global time rescaling. The findings do not contradict known bounds and the recent result that spatial observational data only determine the Markov equivalence class of the underlying graph. In this work, we identify physical assumptions that lift this barrier. The absolute time scale is not identifiable from a single snapshot of any sample size and requires an external clock. For tumor-immune tissue, the results imply that directed cell-cell interactions are in principle recoverable from one section, that the direction cannot be inferred from the mean densities or a covariance matrix, but from the wavenumber dependence of the cross and autospectra, and that a baseline section determines the interaction structure but not the absolute rates.

AI.tldr: A single spatial snapshot's stationary second-order statistics (structure factor S(k)) can generically identify the directed interaction operator A and diffusivity matrix D of a linear reaction-diffusion model, up to one global time rescaling.
AI.motivation: A spatial snapshot captures positions but not the dynamics that produced them. The paper asks what stationary second-order statistics of a snapshot reveal about the underlying linear reaction-diffusion model, especially the directed (pairwise) entries of its interaction operator—and how to lift the known barrier that spatial data only determine a Markov equivalence class of the graph.
AI.method: The observation is the matrix-valued structure factor S(k), treated as a one-parameter family in the diffusion-inherited wavenumber dependence κ=|k|². The authors analyze identifiability of the directed interaction operator A and diffusivity matrix D from {S(κ)}, drawing on physical assumptions to break the Markov-equivalence-class barrier.
AI.result: The directed interaction operator A and diffusivity matrix D are generically identifiable for any number of interacting populations from {S(κ)}, up to a single global time rescaling. Absolute time scale is not identifiable from a single snapshot of any sample size and requires an external clock. Results do not contradict known bounds or the Markov-equivalence-class result.
AI.conclusion: For tumor-immune tissue, directed cell-cell interactions are in principle recoverable from one section. Direction cannot be inferred from mean densities or a covariance matrix, but from the wavenumber dependence of the cross- and autospectra; a baseline section determines interaction structure but not absolute rates.

title: IMPPAT 3.0: An updated FAIR database of phytochemicals and formulations of Indian Medicinal plants
comment: 51 pages, 29 pages of main text and 22 pages of supporting information
summary: Ayurvedic formulations represent a rich source of traditional knowledge, encompassing distinct therapeutic approaches, medicinal ingredients, and underlying principles of drug action. However, systematic integration of this knowledge with standardized modern biomedical terminology and resources remains limited. Here, we present IMPPAT 3.0, an updated version of the Indian Medicinal Plants, Phytochemistry And Therapeutics (IMPPAT: https://cb.imsc.res.in/imppat/) database that extends its scope by incorporating curated and harmonized information on Ayurvedic formulations from authoritative sources, while expanding its coverage of medicinal plants, phytochemicals, and therapeutic use terms. IMPPAT 3.0 further enriches plant and phytochemical information with annotations on clinical trials, patents, bioactivity, protein targets, spectral data, plant image links, and AyuCaRe reports. The compiled data is also organized as IMPPAT-KG, a knowledge graph that enables exploration of relationships among IMPPAT entities. We demonstrate the utility of the resource through a network medicine analysis of single herbal drugs (SHDs) reported for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), revealing significant proximity of their protein targets to RA-associated genes, and pinpointing of phytochemical pairs with potentially complementary effects on RA pathogenesis. In conclusion, by integrating traditional medicinal knowledge, IMPPAT provides a FAIR-compliant ethnopharmacological platform for systematic investigation of Indian medicinal plants and Ayurvedic formulations for drug discovery applications.

AI.tldr: IMPPAT 3.0 is an updated FAIR-compliant ethnopharmacological database integrating Ayurvedic formulations with modern biomedical terminology, plus a knowledge graph (IMPPAT-KG), demonstrated via network medicine analysis of rheumatoid arthritis herbal drugs.
AI.motivation: Ayurvedic formulations hold rich traditional knowledge, but systematic integration with standardized modern biomedical terminology and resources is limited, hindering drug discovery applications.
AI.method: Curated and harmonized Ayurvedic formulation data from authoritative sources; expanded coverage of medicinal plants, phytochemicals, and therapeutic terms; enriched annotations (clinical trials, patents, bioactivity, protein targets, spectral data, image links, AyuCaRe reports); organized data as the IMPPAT-KG knowledge graph; performed network medicine analysis on single herbal drugs for rheumatoid arthritis.
AI.result: Protein targets of RA-reported single herbal drugs showed significant proximity to RA-associated genes, and phytochemical pairs with potentially complementary effects on RA pathogenesis were identified.
AI.conclusion: By integrating traditional medicinal knowledge, IMPPAT 3.0 provides a FAIR-compliant ethnopharmacological platform for systematic investigation of Indian medicinal plants and Ayurvedic formulations for drug discovery.

title: Linear Fitness Subspace in Protein Language Models Enables Sample-Efficient Directed Evolution
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Model-guided directed evolution seeks to identify high-fitness protein variants under limited oracle budgets. Protein language models (PLMs) provide rich representations for this task, but task-agnostic zero-shot scores can be misaligned with a target assay, while supervised search in high-dimensional embedding spaces can make surrogate modeling and uncertainty estimation sample-inefficient. We propose the Linear Fitness Subspace (LFS) hypothesis: within mutation-induced residue-level representation changes, a compact, assay-specific set of directions makes fitness variation linearly accessible from few labeled variants. This is a local, supervision-recoverable statement rather than a claim that protein fitness landscapes or global PLM geometry are universally linear. Building on this observation, we introduce Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES), which estimates an LFS from a small initial sample and performs surrogate modeling, uncertainty estimation, and acquisition in the learned subspace. Across 10 core ProteinGym assays, 87 extended static-validation assays, and an 18-assay budgeted-search evaluation, SGES improves fitness prediction and search efficiency over zero-shot PLMs and recent ML-guided protein optimization baselines. Controlled comparisons with PCA, random projections, label-shuffled PLS, classical mutation features, and acquisition ablations further isolate the benefit of a fitness-aligned site-delta coordinate.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Linear Fitness Subspace (LFS) hypothesis and introduces Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) to improve protein variant fitness prediction and search efficiency under limited oracle budgets.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot PLM scores may be misaligned with target assays, and supervised search in high-dimensional embedding spaces is sample-inefficient for surrogate modeling and uncertainty estimation.
AI.method: SGES estimates an assay-specific LFS from mutation-induced residue-level representation changes using few labeled variants, then performs surrogate modeling, uncertainty estimation, and acquisition within the learned subspace.
AI.result: Across 10 core ProteinGym assays, 87 extended static-validation assays, and an 18-assay budgeted-search evaluation, SGES outperforms zero-shot PLMs and recent ML-guided protein optimization baselines. Ablations isolate the benefit of fitness-aligned site-delta coordinates.
AI.conclusion: A compact, fitness-aligned linear subspace enables efficient, supervision-recoverable protein fitness optimization, improving over existing methods.

title: Mathematical Invariant-Enabled Topological Neural Networks for Molecular and Materials Property Prediction
summary: Existing molecular and materials learning approaches often rely on a limited set of structural representations, which may capture only selected aspects of complex three-dimensional structure. Here, we introduce mathematical invariant-enabled topological neural networks (MITNNs), a framework that represents complex structures through multiple complementary mathematical views and integrates them with topological neural architectures. MITNNs combine multiscale invariants from topology, spectral theory, commutative algebra, differential geometry, and discrete curvature, capturing complementary structural information from the same system. Systematic invariant-subset, architecture-subset, and ensemble analyses show that predictive performance depends on how mathematical representations and neural architectures are paired, with selected combinations outperforming individual models and the aggregation of all available components. Across protein-ligand binding, metal-organic framework properties, mutation-induced protein solubility, and molecular toxicity prediction, MITNN consistently outperforms existing methods. These results establish MITNN as a mathematically multimodal framework for scientific machine learning.

AI.tldr: MITNNs integrate multiple mathematical invariants (topology, spectral theory, commutative algebra, differential geometry, discrete curvature) with topological neural architectures, outperforming existing methods across diverse scientific prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing molecular and materials learning approaches rely on limited structural representations that capture only selected aspects of complex three-dimensional structure, missing complementary structural information.
AI.method: A framework representing complex structures through multiple complementary mathematical views and integrating them with topological neural architectures. Combines multiscale invariants from topology, spectral theory, commutative algebra, differential geometry, and discrete curvature. Includes systematic invariant-subset, architecture-subset, and ensemble analyses.
AI.result: Predictive performance depends on how mathematical representations are paired with neural architectures, with selected combinations outperforming individual models and the aggregation of all components. MITNN consistently outperforms existing methods across protein-ligand binding, metal-organic framework properties, mutation-induced protein solubility, and molecular toxicity prediction.
AI.conclusion: MITNN establishes a mathematically multimodal framework for scientific machine learning.

title: Encoding level-3 semi-directed phylogenetic networks by quarnets and quinnets
summary: Phylogenetic networks generalize phylogenetic trees as models of evolutionary history, allowing lineages to merge as well as to diverge. For many types of genetic data the root position of such a network cannot be recovered, so that only a semi-directed network can be inferred: a mixed graph in which only the edges entering a reticulation vertex are directed. A common strategy for inferring such a network is to first infer the subnetwork it induces on each set of $k\geq 3$ of its leaves, called a $k$-net, and then to assemble these pieces. This can only succeed if the $k$-nets determine the network, in which case that network is said to be encoded by its $k$-nets. Semi-directed networks of level-1 and 2, those whose biconnected components contain at most one, respectively two, reticulations, are known to be encoded by their $4$-nets, or quarnets, whereas level-3 networks are not. Even so, in this paper we show that level-3 semi-directed networks are encoded by their $5$-nets, or quinnets, and we characterize the limitation of quarnets exactly: we show that a single previously reported counterexample captures the only obstruction, every other level-3 network being encoded by its quarnets. Our proofs rest on a collection of encoding results for individual structural features of a network, which we establish for networks of arbitrary level and which are of independent interest.

AI.tldr: Level-3 semi-directed phylogenetic networks are encoded by their 5-nets (quinnets), and the only obstruction to quarnet (4-net) encoding is a single known counterexample.
AI.motivation: Root position of phylogenetic networks often cannot be recovered, so only semi-directed networks can be inferred. Inferring such networks by assembling k-nets requires that the k-nets determine (encode) the network. Level-1 and level-2 networks are known to be encoded by quarnets, but level-3 networks are not, leaving the encoding limits unclear.
AI.method: The paper proves encoding results for individual structural features of semi-directed networks, established for networks of arbitrary level, and uses them to analyze k-net encoding for level-3 networks. It characterizes exactly the limitation of quarnets by identifying the unique obstruction.
AI.result: Level-3 semi-directed networks are encoded by their 5-nets (quinnets). Moreover, a single previously reported counterexample is shown to be the only obstruction to quarnet encoding: every other level-3 network is encoded by its quarnets.
AI.conclusion: Quinnets suffice to uniquely determine level-3 semi-directed networks, and quarnet encoding fails only for one specific counterexample. The structural encoding results for arbitrary-level networks are of independent interest.

title: Effects of Periodic Migration on Selection in Subdivided Populations
summary: Migration and selection jointly shape evolutionary outcomes in spatially structured populations. Migration can vary over time as ecological shifts, such as changes in sea level, alter habitat connectivity. Here, we study the impact of periodic migration on selection within a geographically subdivided population. Using a two-deme Moran model with spatially heterogeneous selection, we analyze a scenario in which a mutant genotype is advantageous in one habitat and disadvantageous in the other. Keeping the time-averaged migration rate fixed, we vary the period, relative phase, and directional asymmetry of migration and examine the resulting steady-state mutant frequency. We find that migration periodicity generally drives the population toward neutrality: relative to constant migration, it decreases the mutant frequency when mutants are advantageous on average and increases it when they are deleterious, without reversing the direction of selection in the parameter regimes examined. This effect is strongest for out-of-phase migration, which models seasonal migration, and is further enhanced by directional asymmetry. The response to the migration period is generally non-monotonic, with an intermediate characteristic period producing the largest deviation from constant-migration behavior under in-phase migration. These results arise from the coupling between migration and local selection in Moran process: temporal modulation of migration changes not only the exchange of individuals between habitats but also the local population composition on which selection acts. Our results show that populations with identical mean migration rates can show different evolutionary outcomes depending on the temporal organization of gene flow.

AI.tldr: Periodic (rather than constant) migration in a two-deme Moran model with heterogeneous selection drives mutant frequency toward neutrality, with the effect maximized for out-of-phase and directionally asymmetric migration and showing a non-monotonic dependence on migration period.
AI.motivation: Migration and selection jointly shape evolution in spatially structured populations, and migration rates fluctuate over time due to ecological shifts (e.g., sea-level changes altering habitat connectivity). Prior work largely assumes constant migration, leaving unclear how the temporal organization of gene flow—holding the time-averaged rate fixed—affects selection outcomes.
AI.method: A two-deme Moran model with spatially heterogeneous selection is used, where a mutant is advantageous in one habitat and disadvantageous in the other. The time-averaged migration rate is held fixed while the period, relative phase, and directional asymmetry of periodic migration are varied; the resulting steady-state mutant frequency is analyzed.
AI.result: Migration periodicity generally pushes the population toward neutrality: compared to constant migration, it lowers mutant frequency when mutants are advantageous on average and raises it when deleterious, without reversing the selection direction in the examined regimes. The effect is strongest for out-of-phase (seasonal) migration and is enhanced by directional asymmetry. The response to period is non-monotonic, with an intermediate characteristic period yielding the largest deviation under in-phase migration.
AI.conclusion: The effects arise from coupling between migration and local selection in the Moran process: temporal modulation changes both individual exchange between habitats and the local population composition on which selection acts. Thus, populations with identical mean migration rates can reach different evolutionary outcomes depending on the temporal organization of gene flow.

title: Neural networks as decision trees: an analytical solution for learning and neural selectivity
summary: Nonlinear neural networks develop structured internal representations, yet how their geometry is determined by the tasks being learned remains poorly understood. Here, we develop an analytical framework for piecewise-linear feedforward and recurrent networks that links learning, activation-region structure, and neural selectivity. We show that, at any stationary point of gradient-aligned learning, a nonlinear network decomposes into local linear regressions over its activation regions. Deviations from the corresponding least-squares solutions are jointly constrained by network weights shared across regions and vanish in the low-error regime, yielding an approximate piecewise least-squares decomposition of the task. This structure admits a decision-tree interpretation, which we recover numerically by fitting trees to predict network activation patterns from the input. We further derive how the regions in which neurons are active determine the task statistics they capture, thereby organizing neural selectivity into distinct subpopulations. The resulting predictions closely match the selectivity geometry observed in simulated networks and two empirical neural datasets. Finally, we show that neural baseline regulates activation pattern diversity, placing networks along a continuum between coarse, generalizing representations and fine-grained, expressive representations. Together, these results establish activation regions as a unifying framework for describing how nonlinear networks decompose task structure into local computations and how those computations can be revealed through neural activity.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analytical framework showing that piecewise-linear networks decompose tasks into local linear regressions over activation regions, yielding a decision-tree interpretation and predicting neural selectivity geometry.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear neural networks develop structured internal representations, but how their geometry is determined by the tasks being learned remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Develops an analytical framework for piecewise-linear feedforward and recurrent networks linking learning, activation-region structure, and neural selectivity. Shows that at stationary points of gradient-aligned learning, networks decompose into local linear regressions over activation regions; deviations from least-squares solutions are constrained by shared weights and vanish in low-error regimes. Derives a decision-tree interpretation (recovered numerically) and analyzes how active regions determine captured task statistics.
AI.result: Predictions closely match selectivity geometry in simulated networks and two empirical neural datasets. Neural baseline is shown to regulate activation pattern diversity, placing networks along a continuum between coarse, generalizing and fine-grained, expressive representations.
AI.conclusion: Activation regions provide a unifying framework for describing how nonlinear networks decompose task structure into local computations and how those computations can be revealed through neural activity.

title: HRPv2: an automated and enhanced method for full-length homology-based R-gene prediction
summary: Motivation: Plant disease resistance genes, particularly those encoding NB-LRR proteins, are important targets for crop improvement. Proteome-based domain or motif searches can only identify NB-LRRs among existing gene models, meaning they cannot recover loci that have been missed or incorrectly predicted by the reference annotation. The full-length, homology-based R-gene prediction (HRP) method circumvents this issue by reconstructing gene models directly on the genome. However, the original implementation of this method requires several separate phases of classification, comparison and filtering operations. Results: HRPv2 is an automated, enhanced version of the original strategy. The labour-intensive, step-by-step curation process used in HRP has been replaced by a reproducible filtering framework. Enhancing two steps of the homology search process has enabled HRPv2 to better account for the specific NB-LRR variability of the genome. Performance validation confirmed that the number of full-length NB-LRRs annotated in both the automatically predicted gene set of the respective genome assembly and the final NB-LRR repertoire has increased in HRPv2 compared to HRP. Availability and implementation: HRPv2 and its associated documentation and reproducible test data are available at https://github.com/AndolfoG/HRPv2. Detailed installation and dependency information is provided in the repository README. A version-pinned Conda package has also been developed and locally validated to provide a reproducible execution environment.

AI.tldr: HRPv2 automates and improves the full-length, homology-based R-gene prediction (HRP) method for identifying NB-LRR resistance genes directly on the genome, replacing manual curation with a reproducible filtering framework and increasing the number of full-length NB-LRRs recovered.
AI.motivation: NB-LRR resistance genes are key targets for crop improvement, but proteome-based searches can only identify them among existing gene models, failing to recover loci missed or mispredicted by reference annotations. The original HRP method addressed this by reconstructing gene models on the genome, but it required several separate, labor-intensive phases of classification, comparison, and filtering.
AI.method: HRPv2 is an automated, enhanced version that replaces the step-by-step manual curation of HRP with a reproducible filtering framework. Two steps of the homology search process were enhanced to better account for the specific NB-LRR variability of the genome.
AI.result: Performance validation showed that HRPv2 increased the number of full-length NB-LRRs annotated, both in the automatically predicted gene set of the respective genome assembly and in the final NB-LRR repertoire, compared to HRP.
AI.conclusion: HRPv2 provides an improved, reproducible, and automated tool for homology-based NB-LRR gene prediction. It is freely available on GitHub with documentation, reproducible test data, and a version-pinned Conda package for a reproducible execution environment.

title: A Time-Resolved Framework for Quantifying Neuronal Network State Transitions
summary: Electrophysiological recordings provide powerful tools for characterizing the dynamics of neuronal networks. In vitro neuronal cultures offer a controlled setting for investigating network responses to diverse interventions, including pharmacological and optogenetic stimulation. However, conventional analyses often reduce electrophysiological activity to aggregate measures calculated over fixed temporal windows, providing only a static representation of the network state. Here, we introduce a comprehensive, multiparametric analytical framework designed to characterize both the temporal evolution of network activity and the transitional states induced by external interventions. The framework combines multiple network discriminators with a compositional analysis that resolves electrode-level responses into excited, inhibited, and unchanged states over successive temporal segments. We apply the framework to electrophysiological recordings obtained under pharmacological interventions with 4-aminopyridine (4-AP), optogenetic stimulation, and additional benchmark conditions. The results demonstrate that the proposed analysis can reveal subtle and transient responses that may be difficult to detect using conventional aggregate measures, including responses to low-dose pharmacological interventions. These findings highlight the value of temporally resolved and compositional analyses for characterizing heterogeneous neuronal network responses in vitro.

AI.tldr: A multiparametric framework characterizes the temporal evolution and transitional states of in vitro neuronal network activity via electrode-level compositional analysis (excited/inhibited/unchanged), revealing subtle and transient responses missed by conventional aggregate measures.
AI.motivation: Conventional electrophysiological analyses reduce activity to aggregate measures over fixed temporal windows, yielding only static network representations and missing subtle, transient, or heterogeneous responses.
AI.method: A comprehensive multiparametric framework combining multiple network discriminators with compositional analysis that resolves electrode-level responses into excited, inhibited, and unchanged states across successive temporal segments. Applied to recordings under 4-AP pharmacological interventions, optogenetic stimulation, and benchmark conditions.
AI.result: The framework revealed subtle and transient responses difficult to detect with conventional aggregate measures, including responses to low-dose pharmacological interventions.
AI.conclusion: Temporally resolved and compositional analyses are valuable for characterizing heterogeneous neuronal network responses in vitro.

title: OncoNoteBERT: A Foundation Representation Model for Natural Language Processing of Real-World Outpatient Oncology Notes
comment: Accepted at the AI at Scale for Clinical Impact (ASCI): Cancer Pathology Foundation Models Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Real-world outpatient oncology notes contain specialised terminology, tumour staging expressions, treatment names, toxicity descriptions, and institution-specific de-identification markers that may not be represented efficiently by general biomedical or adjacent clinical language models. We developed and evaluated oncology-specific BERT-style encoders using a governed UK outpatient oncology corpus comprising 290,026 notes from 21,564 patients treated for lung and head-and-neck cancer. We compared RadBERT and PathologyBERT with two local strategies: OncoNote-RadBERT, produced by continued masked language model pretraining, and OncoNoteBERT, trained from scratch with an oncology WordPiece tokenizer. Models were evaluated using masked language modelling loss and perplexity on the validation set, tokenizer fragmentation metrics, clinical term tokenisation, masked-token probes, and exploratory representation analysis. Both external encoders fit the oncology corpus poorly in zero-shot evaluation (perplexity 113.04 for RadBERT; 2035.03 for PathologyBERT), while continued pretraining produced the strongest fit (2.10 for OncoNote-RadBERT). OncoNoteBERT achieved perplexity 2.83 but produced the most efficient tokenisation, with lower subword fertility and shorter normalised sequence length. It also returned a clinically acceptable prediction for 12 of 13 masked-token probes, compared with 7 of 13 for OncoNote-RadBERT. This divergence between corpus-level fit and masked-token performance was partly attributable to tokenizer fragmentation rather than learned semantics alone. Both locally developed models represented the institutional placeholder as a single learnable token. These findings show that continued adaptation and bespoke tokenisation provide complementary benefits, and that representation-layer design matters before adjacent-domain encoders are applied to oncology NLP.

AI.tldr: Oncology-specific BERT encoders were developed on 290,026 UK outpatient lung and head-and-neck cancer notes, showing continued pretraining and bespoke tokenisation offer complementary benefits over external adjacent-domain models.
AI.motivation: Real-world outpatient oncology notes contain specialised terminology, tumour staging, treatment names, toxicity descriptions, and institution-specific de-identification markers that general biomedical or adjacent clinical language models may not represent efficiently.
AI.method: Built two local strategies on a governed UK oncology corpus: OncoNote-RadBERT (continued masked language model pretraining) and OncoNoteBERT (trained from scratch with an oncology WordPiece tokenizer). Compared against RadBERT and PathologyBERT using MLM loss/perplexity, tokenizer fragmentation, clinical term tokenisation, masked-token probes, and representation analysis.
AI.result: External encoders fit poorly zero-shot (perplexity 113.04 RadBERT; 2035.03 PathologyBERT); continued pretraining gave best fit (2.10 OncoNote-RadBERT). OncoNoteBERT reached perplexity 2.83 with most efficient tokenisation (lower subword fertility, shorter sequences) and clinically acceptable predictions on 12/13 masked-token probes vs 7/13 for OncoNote-RadBERT. Both local models represented the institutional placeholder as a single learnable token.
AI.conclusion: Continued adaptation and bespoke tokenisation provide complementary benefits; the divergence between corpus-level fit and masked-token performance is partly due to tokenizer fragmentation rather than learned semantics alone. Representation-layer design matters before applying adjacent-domain encoders to oncology NLP.

title: CANDLE: Cortical Null-Space Decomposition for Noninvasive Brain Source Imaging
summary: Electrophysiological source imaging (ESI) aims to estimate cortical source activity from noninvasive electrophysiological measurements such as electroencephalogram (EEG). However, ESI is fundamentally ill-posed because source activity is substantially higher-dimensional than sensor observations, resulting in non-unique solutions. Recent learning-based approaches address this ambiguity by learning data-driven source priors, yet they often struggle to generalize across subject-specific cortical geometries. To address this, we propose CANDLE, a learning-based ESI model that estimates source activity on subject-specific cortical geometries. CANDLE learns a prior over the null space induced by the source-to-sensor mapping derived from T1-weighted MRI, restricting learning to unobservable source components while preserving geometric constraints. To train CANDLE, we develop a whole-brain simulator spanning over 1,100 subject-specific cortical geometries with source configurations derived from over 26,000 statistical brain maps. Trained exclusively on simulated data, CANDLE outperformed prior ESI methods on simulated source activity estimation and generalized to two empirical tasks: (i) intracranial stimulation localization from simultaneously recorded scalp EEG and (ii) epileptogenic zone estimation from presurgical interictal EEG. Our project page is available at https://candle-esi.pages.dev}{https://candle-esi.pages.dev.

AI.tldr: CANDLE is a learning-based electrophysiological source imaging model that estimates source activity on subject-specific cortical geometries by learning a prior over the null space of the source-to-sensor mapping, achieving strong generalization from simulated training to empirical tasks.
AI.motivation: ESI is fundamentally ill-posed due to the far higher dimensionality of source activity compared to sensor observations, yielding non-unique solutions. Existing learning-based methods that learn data-driven source priors struggle to generalize across subject-specific cortical geometries.
AI.method: CANDLE learns a prior over the null space induced by the source-to-sensor mapping derived from T1-weighted MRI, restricting learning to unobservable source components while preserving geometric constraints. It is trained on a whole-brain simulator spanning over 1,100 subject-specific cortical geometries with source configurations from over 26,000 statistical brain maps.
AI.result: Trained exclusively on simulated data, CANDLE outperformed prior ESI methods on simulated source activity estimation and generalized to two empirical tasks: intracranial stimulation localization from simultaneously recorded scalp EEG, and epileptogenic zone estimation from presurgical interictal EEG.
AI.conclusion: CANDLE demonstrates that null-space-restricted learning on subject-specific geometries enables generalizable ESI, bridging simulated training and real-world clinical tasks. Project page: https://candle-esi.pages.dev

title: ReGraph: A Computational Account of Emergent Generalization in the "what" and "where" Dual Visual Streams
summary: Where generalization capacity--the ability to extract context-invariant relational structures--first emerges remains a central question in AI and neuroscience. The foundation for this capacity lies upstream of the hippocampus, within the entorhinal cortex, where parallel pathways dissociate relational structure in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) from sensory content in the lateral entorhinal cortex. However, as Eichenbaum argued, such factorization likely originates earlier, driven by the segregation of the dorsal ('where') and ventral ('what') visual streams. Supporting this, grid-like firing patterns--a signature of MEC (context-invariant codes)--also appear in preceding neocortical regions along the dorsal pathway. Yet, how such representations are computationally formed along upstream pathways remains unknown. To investigate this in silico, we developed ReGraph, a recurrent dual-stream graph model with biological inductive biases, including retina-driven stream-specialized encoding, dorsal-to-ventral modulation, and dynamic lateral connectivity. Trained on the action benchmark Something-Something V2, ReGraph revealed a pathway-specific emergence of relational mapping: context-invariant codes and grid-like spatial bases uniquely co-emerged along the extended dorsal stream. In contrast, their absence in single-stream, unmodulated variants, and standard baselines implies that these inductive biases are prerequisites for relational structures. Crucially, our post-hoc analyses demonstrated that these grid-like bases serve as reusable routing templates for information processing via lateral connectivity. Together, our findings provide a computational account that generalization may not be a faculty that emerges abruptly within a dedicated region, but a property that already takes shape as sensory information is parsed into factorized streams of hierarchical visual processing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReGraph, a recurrent dual-stream graph model with biological inductive biases, to show that context-invariant relational codes and grid-like spatial bases emerge along the extended dorsal visual stream during visual processing.
AI.motivation: Understanding where generalization capacity first emerges is a central question in AI and neuroscience. While the entorhinal cortex factorizes relational structure (MEC) from sensory content (LEC), Eichenbaum argued this factorization likely originates earlier, driven by the segregation of dorsal ('where') and ventral ('what') visual streams. However, how such representations are computationally formed along upstream pathways remains unknown.
AI.method: The authors developed ReGraph, a recurrent dual-stream graph model with biological inductive biases: retina-driven stream-specialized encoding, dorsal-to-ventral modulation, and dynamic lateral connectivity. It was trained on the action benchmark Something-Something V2, with comparisons against single-stream, unmodulated variants and standard baselines, plus post-hoc analyses.
AI.result: ReGraph revealed a pathway-specific emergence of relational mapping: context-invariant codes and grid-like spatial bases uniquely co-emerged along the extended dorsal stream. These were absent in single-stream, unmodulated variants and standard baselines, implying the inductive biases are prerequisites for relational structures. Post-hoc analyses showed the grid-like bases serve as reusable routing templates via lateral connectivity.
AI.conclusion: Generalization may not be a faculty emerging abruptly within a dedicated region, but a property that already takes shape as sensory information is parsed into factorized streams of hierarchical visual processing.

title: Confidence-Ordering Reversal under Contextual Priors in Neural Decoding
summary: Contextual priors improve neural-to-language decoding by reshaping candidate scores. However, confidence is read from the same reshaped scores, so the errors a prior leaves behind can become more confident with no change in accuracy to reveal it. We study how a prior shapes confidence in speech retrieval on MEG-MASC and MOUS using local decoding scores, a contextual prior combined by additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as confidence. Among initially incorrect predictions, we find a confidence-ordering reversal: a larger margin makes a repair more likely when the correct candidate starts near the top of the local ranking, but less likely when it starts lower. On MEG-MASC, pooled correctness AUROC is 0.87, yet AUROC separating repairs from residual errors falls from 0.70 at initial ranks 2-3 to 0.39 at ranks 21-50. Errors starting beyond rank 20, inside the reversed region, make up 46.6% of all post-fusion errors. We propose a score-level account: a repair must first close the correct candidate's initial deficit, limiting its final margin, whereas a residual error can build a large margin between two incorrect candidates. A causal intervention that changes only the fusion weight moves the reversal to deeper ranks as predicted. Under a word-level LM prior, it keeps moving after accuracy gain peaks, so a weight chosen for accuracy does not settle confidence. Reading local and prior scores separately improves selective decoding: the decoder answers on 74.5% of windows instead of 56.7%, while 92% of output sets still contain the correct candidate. Confidence after contextual fusion should retain the local and contextual evidence behind each prediction, not just the fused scores. Project website: https://confidencereversal.github.io/; Code: https://github.com/AmadeusFake/NeuDecodingConfReversal

AI.tldr: Contextual priors reshape decoding scores in ways that can make errors more confident without changing accuracy. The paper identifies a "confidence-ordering reversal" in fused top-two margins and proposes separating local and prior scores for better selective decoding.
AI.motivation: Contextual priors improve neural-to-language decoding, but confidence is read from the same reshaped scores, so residual errors from the prior can become more confident without any accuracy change to reveal it. This confidence miscalibration under contextual fusion is underexplored for speech retrieval.
AI.method: The authors study MEG-MASC and MOUS speech retrieval using local decoding scores, a contextual prior combined via additive shallow fusion, and the fused top-two margin as confidence. They analyze AUROC separating repairs from residual errors by initial rank, propose a score-level account of the reversal, and run a causal intervention varying only the fusion weight.
AI.result: A confidence-ordering reversal appears: larger margin makes repairs more likely when the correct candidate starts near the top but less likely when it starts lower. Pooled correctness AUROC is 0.87 on MEG-MASC, but repair-vs-residual AUROC falls from 0.70 at ranks 2-3 to 0.39 at ranks 21-50. Errors beyond rank 20 (in the reversed region) are 46.6% of post-fusion errors. The causal intervention moves the reversal to deeper ranks as predicted, and it keeps moving past the accuracy peak. Reading local and prior scores separately lets the decoder answer on 74.5% of windows (vs 56.7%) with 92% correct-candidate coverage.
AI.conclusion: Confidence after contextual fusion should retain the local and contextual evidence behind each prediction, not just the fused scores. Separating these score components improves selective decoding reliability.

title: From the Drosophila Visual Connectome to General-Purpose Computer Vision
summary: Biological connectomes encode structured solutions to visual computation that may provide reusable inductive biases for artificial vision. We develop ConnectomeX around FlyVision, a trainable architecture that preserves parallel ON/OFF processing, recurrent computation and population-level graph interaction while scaling model capacity across tasks. FlyVision reached 99.34% accuracy on MNIST with 80,608 parameters and 78.03% on CIFAR-10 with 81,408 parameters. On ImageNet-1K, FlyVision Base and Large reached 60.79% and 66.25% top-1 accuracy with 1.8 and 3.7 million parameters, while a Large local-k7 model with a learned low-frequency branch reached 66.53%, compared with 69.25% for ResNet18 with 11.7 million parameters. On a 22-class skin-disease benchmark, FlyVision Large achieved 63.78% accuracy and 95.28% macro-AUROC with 2.99 million parameters. In four-class chest radiography, ImageNet-pretrained FlyVision Base and Large reached 92.60% and 92.76% accuracy with 1.33 and 2.97 million parameters, compared with 91.56% for ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 with 11.18 million. BrainAGE extends FlyVision to volumetric T1-weighted MRI by applying a shared ImageNet-pretrained FlyVision Large encoder to 24 sagittal, coronal and axial slices per scan and combining slice-level age estimates by confidence-modulated Gaussian voting. On 433 held-out scans, three-axis fusion achieved a mean absolute error of 5.98 years and R^2 = 0.868. Across the 224x224 classification tasks, the best FlyVision configuration remained within three percentage points of ResNet18 on ImageNet-1K and skin-disease classification and exceeded it on chest radiography with substantially fewer parameters. These results show that a conserved connectome-informed computation can scale from compact recognition to large-scale natural and biomedical vision.

AI.tldr: ConnectomeX introduces FlyVision, a connectome-informed trainable vision architecture that scales across tasks, matching or exceeding ResNet18 on several benchmarks with far fewer parameters, and extends to volumetric MRI via a BrainAGE model.
AI.motivation: Biological connectomes encode structured solutions to visual computation that could provide reusable inductive biases for artificial vision, motivating a scalable architecture derived from these principles.
AI.method: FlyVision preserves parallel ON/OFF processing, recurrent computation, and population-level graph interaction while scaling capacity. Variants (Base/Large, local-k7 with learned low-frequency branch) are evaluated. BrainAGE applies a shared ImageNet-pretrained FlyVision Large encoder to 24 slices per axis (sagittal, coronal, axial) and fuses slice-level age estimates via confidence-modulated Gaussian voting.
AI.result: MNIST 99.34% (80,608 params); CIFAR-10 78.03% (81,408 params). ImageNet-1K: Base 60.79%, Large 66.25%, Large local-k7 66.53% vs ResNet18 69.25% (11.7M params). Skin-disease (22-class): 63.78% acc, 95.28% macro-AUROC (2.99M). Chest radiography (4-class): 92.60%/92.76% vs ResNet18 91.56% (11.18M). BrainAGE: MAE 5.98 years, R^2=0.868 on 433 scans.
AI.conclusion: A conserved connectome-informed computation can scale from compact recognition to large-scale natural and biomedical vision, staying within three points of ResNet18 on ImageNet-1K and skin-disease while surpassing it on chest radiography with far fewer parameters.

title: Information-Dense Synthesis for Molecular Discovery
summary: Machine learning can accelerate molecular discovery by designing molecules and planning experiments. However, many scientific challenges demand molecules with very rare properties, and in this sparse setting, existing algorithms offer little gain over random guessing. We propose a method to efficiently search large regions of molecular space using algorithmically controlled stochastic synthesis. Rather than design, make and test individual molecules, we design and make complex mixtures, test them as a pool, then deconvolute the molecule-activity map. We optimize synthesis to encode maximal information. Theoretically, this approach can reduce the number of experiments required to find the optimal molecule among $d$ candidates from $\mathcal{O}(d)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log d)$ or $\mathcal{O}(1)$. In simulation, on estimated protein fitness landscapes, it finds active molecules with an order of magnitude fewer experiments than existing Bayesian optimization methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a stochastic synthesis-based search method that designs and tests complex molecular mixtures instead of individual molecules, reducing experiments to find rare-property molecules from O(d) to O(log d) or O(1).
AI.motivation: Discovering molecules with very rare properties is challenging; existing machine learning algorithms offer little benefit over random guessing in such sparse settings.
AI.method: Algorithmically controlled stochastic synthesis: rather than designing, making, and testing individual molecules, the method designs and makes complex mixtures, tests them as a pool, and deconvolutes the molecule-activity map, optimizing synthesis to encode maximal information.
AI.result: Theoretically reduces the experiments to find the optimal molecule among d candidates from O(d) to O(log d) or O(1). In simulation on estimated protein fitness landscapes, it finds active molecules with an order of magnitude fewer experiments than existing Bayesian optimization methods.
AI.conclusion: Pool-based stochastic synthesis and deconvolution provides a far more experiment-efficient approach for discovering rare-property molecules than conventional per-molecule design and testing or Bayesian optimization.

title: Language-model ratings of depression reflect the rater more than the patient
summary: Depression has no diagnostic blood test. Language models promise tireless, consistent assessment, but can accurate raters disagree about individuals? We pre-registered 880 language-model raters, crossing 11 open models with prompting and scoring choices, and applied them to 189 interviews against the eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire. Model choice explained 30.0% of summed-symptom score variance, stable participant differences 10.5%. Two randomly drawn raters with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) >= 0.70 disagreed on screening decisions for 40% of participants, on average. Average over-rating governed how many were flagged, yet equal-capacity raters chose differently for about one participant in five. A locked analysis of 86 new interviews reproduced the main pre-registered findings. Exploratory recalibration with 40 labelled participants raised accuracy from about 60% to 75% and halved disagreement, leaving one participant in five decided differently. Calibration repaired much of the rater dependence without securing agreement about individuals.

AI.tldr: Language-model raters of depression screening can be individually accurate (AUC ≥ 0.70) yet disagree on whom to flag; recalibration improves accuracy but cannot secure agreement on individuals.
AI.motivation: Depression lacks a diagnostic blood test. Language models promise tireless, consistent assessment, but it is unclear whether accurate raters can still disagree about individuals.
AI.method: Pre-registered 880 language-model raters (11 open models crossed with prompting and scoring choices) applied to 189 interviews against the eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire; a locked replication on 86 new interviews; exploratory recalibration with 40 labelled participants.
AI.result: Model choice explained 30.0% of summed-symptom score variance; stable participant differences 10.5%. Two random raters with AUC ≥ 0.70 disagreed on screening decisions for ~40% of participants. Equal-capacity raters chose differently for about one in five. Recalibration raised accuracy ~60% to 75% and halved disagreement, still leaving one in five decided differently.
AI.conclusion: Recalibration repaired much of the rater dependence but did not secure agreement about individuals; accurate raters can disagree substantially on individual screening decisions.

title: Sliding-scale Insulin Does Not Control Steroid-induced Hyperglycemia in a Non-diabetic Patient, No Matter How You Tune It
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to Communications Medicine
summary: Sliding-scale correction insulin is the standard hospital response to high blood glucose. Its constants were derived in people who secrete no insulin, yet it is routinely ordered for patients whose own secretion is intact. We represent the correction rule as a proportional controller with a deadband, sampled four-hourly, acting on a glucose model built from published physiology, including pancreatic feedback. We derive the sensitivity of glucose to exogenous insulin, evaluate it in 4,995 virtual patients spanning published parameter ranges, and calibrate the model to a non-diabetic adolescent receiving high-dose corticosteroids and parenteral nutrition, with 45 bedside glucose measurements. Here we show that endogenous regulation restores glucose with a time constant of 11.5 minutes, against 64 minutes for injected insulin to peak, so most of each dose replaces the patient's own secretion and the ordered rule moves mean glucose by less than 1.5 mg/dL. The ordered correction factor exceeds per-unit potency in every virtual patient. Because potency falls as glucose rises, in 99.5% of virtual patients no constant correction factor is both effective at 190 mg/dL and free of overshoot at 110 mg/dL; the mismatch exceeds 25% in 79% and grows with the glucose of half-maximal secretion. Four-hour sampling is phase-locked to dextrose in medication diluents and misses the resulting excursions. When endogenous secretion is intact, the sliding scale fails for structural reasons that retuning cannot fix. A continuous insulin infusion co-delivered with the dextrose and adjusted once daily on mean glucose matches what four-hour monitoring can measure.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that sliding-scale correction insulin is structurally ineffective in patients with intact endogenous insulin secretion, because the patient's own rapid pancreatic feedback dominates and most of each injected dose merely replaces endogenous secretion.
AI.motivation: Sliding-scale correction insulin was derived from people who secrete no insulin, yet it is routinely ordered for patients whose own secretion is intact. The authors question whether the correction rule can work under these mismatched conditions.
AI.method: They model the correction rule as a sampled proportional controller with a deadband (four-hourly) acting on a glucose model built from published physiology including pancreatic feedback. They derive glucose sensitivity to exogenous insulin, evaluate it in 4,995 virtual patients across published parameter ranges, and calibrate to a non-diabetic adolescent on high-dose corticosteroids and parenteral nutrition with 45 bedside glucose measurements.
AI.result: Endogenous regulation restores glucose with an 11.5-minute time constant versus 64 minutes for injected insulin to peak, so most of each dose replaces the patient's own secretion and the ordered rule moves mean glucose by less than 1.5 mg/dL. The correction factor exceeds per-unit potency in every virtual patient. Because potency falls as glucose rises, in 99.5% of patients no constant factor is both effective at 190 mg/dL and overshoot-free at 110 mg/dL; the mismatch exceeds 25% in 79% and grows with the glucose of half-maximal secretion. Four-hour sampling is phase-locked to dextrose in diluents and misses the resulting excursions.
AI.conclusion: When endogenous secretion is intact, the sliding scale fails for structural reasons that retuning cannot fix. A continuous insulin infusion co-delivered with dextrose and adjusted once daily on mean glucose matches what four-hour monitoring can measure.

title: Neural Petri flows for chemical reactions
summary: Petri nets have been used to describe chemical processes such as reactions.They map well to chemistry: Places are the bonds between atoms and the free valence of each atom, a token is a unit of bond order, a transition forms or breaks a bond, the conserved quantities are the valence budgets of the atoms, and the enabling rule is the valence rule. These semantics are not guaranteed by learned models of reactions or neural networks that are built on Petri nets that use the net as a scaffold for message passing. Here, we ask what architecture remains a Petri net for every value of its weights. We find the answer in the theory, where all semantics of a net share the firing form $m^\prime=m+Cσ$, locality, as enabling reads only the inputs of a transition, and the enabling rule, and we prove that conservation forces the firing form and that non-negativity forces the enabling rule on local rate laws. This leaves free the rate law, which is the propensity of each transition to fire. We introduce Neural Petri Flow, which learns this rate law, or a readout for classification, and hard-wires the rest as parameter-free layers. On what we denote a valence net, atom mapping, reaction classification, and forward prediction become three tasks on one firing vector. Without training, the minimum firing vector maps 88.8% of the curated Golden set against 85.6% for RXNMapper, and 88.7 against 77.9% of the enzymatic reactions of EnzymeMap. On USPTO-480K, NPF trained on these firing vectors predicts 87.7% of the products and 67.4% when trained on a 1% subset of the training reactions. EC numbers of ECREACT are predicted at the third level for 90.2% of reactions, 5.6 points ahead of the best published method. With electrons as tokens, the same token game predicts 90.5% of the elementary steps of FlowER first, ahead of the published baseline, and every top-1 prediction is a valid molecule without a filter.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Neural Petri Flow (NPF), a hard-wired Petri-net architecture for chemistry where all net semantics are preserved for every weight value, leaving only the rate law learnable. On a valence net, atom mapping, reaction classification, and forward prediction reduce to tasks on one firing vector, achieving state-of-the-art results without training or filters.
AI.motivation: Petri nets map naturally to chemistry (places=bonds/valences, tokens=bond order, transitions=bond changes, enabling=valence rule), but learned models and neural networks using Petri nets only as message-passing scaffolds do not guarantee these semantics. The paper asks which architecture remains a true Petri net for every value of its weights.
AI.method: They derive the theory showing all net semantics share the firing form m'=m+Cσ, locality, and the enabling rule; conservation forces the firing form and non-negativity forces the enabling rule on local rate laws. This leaves only the rate law free. Neural Petri Flow learns this rate law (or a classification readout) and hard-wires the rest as parameter-free layers. On a "valence net," atom mapping, reaction classification, and forward prediction become three tasks on one firing vector. The same token game also works with electrons as tokens.
AI.result: Without training, minimum firing vector maps 88.8% of Golden set vs 85.6% for RXNMapper, and 88.7% vs 77.9% for EnzymeMap enzymatic reactions. On USPTO-480K, NPF predicts 87.7% of products, and 67.4% when trained on only 1% of reactions. ECREACT EC numbers predicted at third level for 90.2% (5.6 points ahead of best published). With electrons as tokens, predicts 90.5% of FlowER elementary steps, ahead of baseline, with every top-1 prediction a valid molecule without a filter.
AI.conclusion: Neural Petri Flow is a principled architecture that preserves full Petri-net semantics by hard-wiring conservation and enabling rules while learning only rate laws, unifying atom mapping, classification, and prediction on a single firing vector and achieving strong results across multiple chemistry tasks.
